name: Hans Hollein
bio:
Hans Hollein (1934–2014) was an Austrian architect and designer and a key figure of postmodern architecture. Born in Vienna, he studied in Clemens Holzmeister's master class at the Academy of Fine Arts Vienna, then at the Illinois Institute of Technology and the University of California, Berkeley. He opened his own office in Vienna in 1964, designed objects for the Memphis Group and Alessi, and received the Pritzker Prize in 1985.

Among his early small works is the Retti Candle Shop in Vienna (1965), with a façade of anodised aluminium. His competition win for Museum Abteiberg in Mönchengladbach (1982) brought him international fame, and the building is seen as a high point of postmodern design. The Haas House in Vienna (1990) stands beside St Stephen's Cathedral and has been controversial for its contrast with it. The Museum für Moderne Kunst in Frankfurt (1991) fills a triangular plot, which earned it the nickname "piece of cake". At Vulcania in Auvergne (2002) he finally built the underground museum he had first proposed for a Guggenheim in Salzburg. Hans Hollein's buildings are studied for postmodern collage in the historic city.

name: Herman Hertzberger
bio:
Herman Hertzberger (born 1932) is a Dutch architect and teacher, and with Aldo van Eyck one of the leaders of Dutch Structuralism in the 1960s and 1970s. Born in Amsterdam, he studied at the Delft University of Technology, where he was a professor from 1970 to 1999, and from 1959 to 1963 he edited the magazine Forum with van Eyck and Jaap Bakema. He described his approach as "architecture as half-product" and "open structures", and wrote Lessons for Students in Architecture (1991). He received the RIBA Royal Gold Medal in 2012.

His built work runs from the Weesperflat in Amsterdam (1966) to the Chassé Theater in Breda (1995). The eight experimental Diagoon Houses in Delft (1970) were designed for their residents' participation, and the Centraal Beheer offices in Apeldoorn (1972), for an insurance company, became a key work of Structuralism, as Muziekcentrum Vredenburg in Utrecht (1979) was a 5,000-capacity concert venue whose main hall survives inside the new TivoliVredenburg. Herman Hertzberger's buildings are studied for structures that users can take over.

name: Hiroshi Hara
bio:
Hiroshi Hara (1936–2025) was a Japanese architect and writer on architecture, known for large public buildings including Kyoto Station and the Umeda Sky Building. He studied at the University of Tokyo, earning a doctorate in engineering in 1964, and taught there until 1997, becoming professor at its Institute of Industrial Science in 1982. From 1970 he worked with Atelier Φ, renamed Hiroshi Hara + Atelier Φ in 1999. His theoretical essays on architecture and cities include "Discrete City".

The Iida City Museum (1988) followed a run of museums, schools and houses in the 1980s. The Umeda Sky Building in Osaka (1993) is two 40-storey towers joined at their top two floors by bridges across an open atrium, crowned by the Floating Garden Observatory. Kyoto Station Building (1997) is among his best-known works, followed by the Miyagi Prefectural Library in Sendai (1998) and the Sapporo Dome (2001), a football stadium used for the 2002 FIFA World Cup. He also built a series of experimental houses in Latin America, in Montevideo, Córdoba and La Paz. Hiroshi Hara's buildings are studied for treating large buildings as cities.

name: Junzo Sakakura
bio:
Junzo Sakakura (1901–1969) was a Japanese architect and one of the important members of the modernist movement in Japan. Born in Gifu Prefecture, he studied art history at Tokyo Imperial University and in 1930 joined Le Corbusier's atelier in Paris, rising during seven years there from job architect to chief of the studio. His Japanese Pavilion for the 1937 Paris Exposition, a grey box on black pilotis with ramps and a free plan, won the exhibition's Grand Prix. Back in Japan he founded his own practice, and with Kunio Maekawa and Takamasa Yoshizaka he carried out Le Corbusier's National Museum of Western Art in Tokyo (1959).

His first major building in Japan, the Museum of Modern Art, Kamakura (Kamakura Bunkakan Tsurugaoka Museum) (1951), lifts a white box of galleries on thin steel pilotis beside a lake in the grounds of the Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine, over a ground floor of Oya stone. Civic and commercial buildings followed: Hashima City Hall (1959), the Yokohama Silk Center (1959) and the Kure City Hall and Municipal Auditorium (1962). Junzo Sakakura's buildings are studied for Le Corbusier's ideas carried into post-war Japan.

name: Lúcio Costa
bio:
Lúcio Costa (1902–1998) was a Brazilian architect and urban planner, best known for the Pilot Plan of Brasília. Born in Toulon, France, to Brazilian parents, he was schooled in England and Switzerland and graduated in architecture in Rio de Janeiro in 1924. After early work in an eclectic manner he turned to modernism in 1929. From 1937 he worked for Brazil's national heritage service, later leading it. He is associated with joining traditional Brazilian forms and building methods to the modernism of Le Corbusier.

For the heritage service he designed the Museu das Missões in Rio Grande do Sul (1940), built from material taken from the ruins of a Jesuit mission. The Gustavo Capanema Palace in Rio (1945), designed with Oscar Niemeyer, Roberto Burle Marx and others with Le Corbusier as consultant, was the first modernist public building in the Americas, raised on pilotis and shaded by adjustable brise-soleil. The Parque Guinle housing in Rio (1954) followed. His 1957 competition plan laid Brasília out as two crossing axes, and on its Monumental Axis he built the 224-metre Brasília TV Tower (1967).

name: Luigi Moretti
bio:
Luigi Moretti (1907–1973) was an Italian architect from Rome, credited as an inventor of parametric architecture. He graduated with honours from the Royal School of Architecture in Rome in 1929 and in the 1930s became technical director of the Fascist youth organisation, designing its youth centres and the plan of the Foro Mussolini, now the Foro Italico. In 1945 he was arrested for his collaboration with fascism and briefly imprisoned. In 1957 he founded an institute to study "parametric" architecture, applying mathematical methods to design in a way that anticipated the use of computers.

At the Foro he planned the Stadium of the Cypresses, which other architects later enlarged into the Stadio Olimpico (1953). The Casa del Girasole in Rome (1950) is seen as an early example of postmodern architecture. For the developer General Real Estate he designed the Tour de la Bourse in Montreal (1964), with Pier Luigi Nervi, briefly the tallest building in Canada, and the Watergate Complex in Washington, D.C. (1971), whose curved blocks later gave their name to the political scandal. Late work took him to Algeria, where he designed the Hôtel El Aurassi (1975).

name: Luis Barragán
bio:
Luis Barragán (1902–1988) was a Mexican architect and engineer whose houses and gardens have influenced architects around the world. Born in Guadalajara, he trained as an engineer there and travelled in Spain and France, where he discovered the gardens and writings of Ferdinand Bac and briefly met Le Corbusier. He practised in Guadalajara from 1927 and in Mexico City from 1936. Turning away from functionalism, he sought an "emotional architecture", writing that "any work of architecture which does not express serenity is a mistake", and worked with raw stone and wood, strong colour and hidden sources of light. In 1980 he became the second winner of the Pritzker Prize.

His own home, Casa Luis Barragán in Mexico City (1948), became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004. With the sculptor Mathias Goeritz he planned the Torres de Satélite (1958), five tall towers marking a new suburb. Cuadra San Cristóbal (1968), an equestrian estate, and Casa Gilardi (1976) are among his best-known later works, and the bright reddish-orange Faro del Comercio in Monterrey (1984) was built from his design.

name: Mario Pani
bio:
Mario Pani (1911–1993) was a Mexican architect and urban planner who shaped much of modern Mexico City during the years of fast growth known as the Mexican Miracle. Born in Mexico City and raised in Europe, he studied in Genoa, Milan and Paris, finishing at the École des Beaux-Arts. In 1938 he started the journal Arquitectura México, which ran until 1979, and in 1946 he founded the National College of Architects. He introduced the International Style to Mexico and was the first to promote large housing tower blocks, the multifamiliares, following Le Corbusier's urban principles.

The Centro Urbano Presidente Alemán (1949) is one of his large housing complexes in the city. With Enrique del Moral he designed Ciudad Universitaria, UNAM (1954), the main campus of the national university, with its Olympic Stadium, faculties and Central Library. Later came the Nonoalco-Tlatelolco housing estate, with the Torre Insignia (Banobras Tower) (1962), on completion the second tallest building in Mexico, which holds a carillon of 47 bells. Its Plaza de las Tres Culturas (1966) sets the archaeological site of Tlatelolco, a 16th-century college and modern housing side by side.

name: McKim, Mead & White
bio:
McKim, Mead & White was an American architecture firm based in New York City that came to define the ideals of the American Renaissance around 1900. Its founding partners were Charles Follen McKim (1847–1909), William Rutherford Mead (1846–1928), and Stanford White (1853–1906). Their work applied Beaux-Arts principles of classical design, drawing and proportion, and after 1893 the ideas of the City Beautiful movement. White was murdered in 1906, McKim died in 1909 and Mead retired in 1919, but later partners carried the firm on until 1961, with buildings across the United States and in Canada, Cuba and Italy.

McKim's design for the Boston Public Library, McKim Building (1895) won the firm a new circle of institutional clients. The Morgan Library & Museum in New York (1906), built in marble as the private library of the banker J. P. Morgan, followed. The Manhattan Municipal Building (1914) was one of the last works of the City Beautiful in New York, and the James A. Farley Building (Moynihan Train Hall) (1914), a post office fronted by twenty Corinthian columns 16 metres tall, stood beside their original Pennsylvania Station.

name: Otto Wagner
bio:
Otto Wagner (1841–1918) was an Austrian architect, furniture designer and urban planner, a leading member of the Vienna Secession and the wider Art Nouveau movement. Born in Penzing, Vienna, he trained in Vienna and in Berlin under a student of Karl Friedrich Schinkel, and spent his early career building in revival styles along the Ringstrasse. In Modern Architecture (1896) he wrote that "only that which is practical can be beautiful". As professor at the Vienna Academy of Fine Arts he taught students including Josef Hoffmann and Rudolph Schindler.

From 1894 he was artistic director of the Vienna Stadtbahn (1901), the city railway, designing its bridges, viaducts and stations down to the lamps and signs. The Karlsplatz Stadtbahn Pavilions (1899), a pair of metal-framed pavilions faced in marble with gilded sunflower patterns, are its best-known stations. The Majolikahaus (1899) wraps a block of flats in glazed tiles with floral designs. In his later works the ornament became geometric: the Austrian Postal Savings Bank (1906) fixes marble slabs with aluminium rivets that are purely decorative, and the Kirche am Steinhof (1907) crowns a psychiatric hospital.

name: Populous
bio:
Populous is an American architecture firm, based in Kansas City, Missouri, that designs stadiums, arenas, convention centres and major events. It began in 1983 as a sports group of eight architects within the firm HOK, later called HOK Sport, merged with the London and Brisbane practice LOBB Partnership in 1998, and became independent through a management buyout in 2009 under its present name. In the 1990s, starting with Oriole Park at Camden Yards in Baltimore, it led a new era of "retro" ballparks drawing on each city's history and older classic grounds.

The firm finished the design and oversaw construction of the London Stadium (2011), built for the 2012 Olympics. The Aviva Stadium in Dublin (2010) was designed with Scott Tallon Walker, and the Forsyth Barr Stadium in Dunedin, New Zealand (2011), with Jasmax, roofed in 20,500 square metres of clear ETFE. At Lusail Stadium in Qatar (2021), the largest venue of the 2022 FIFA World Cup, Populous designed the seating bowl with Foster + Partners. It also worked on the 68,700-seat Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium in Rabat (2025).

name: Rafael Viñoly
bio:
Rafael Viñoly (1944–2023) was a Uruguayan-born architect based in New York. Born in Montevideo and raised in Buenos Aires, he studied at the University of Buenos Aires and in 1964 co-founded a practice there that became one of the largest in South America. He moved to the United States in 1978 and in 1983 founded Rafael Viñoly Architects in New York. Admirers called him "a serene functionalist and a master of institutional design"; New York magazine's Curbed remembered him as "prolific and polarizing".

The Tokyo International Forum (1996), won in a 1989 international competition, brought him to international prominence; the New York Times critic Herbert Muschamp called it "a monument to the idea of openness". 20 Fenchurch Street in London (2014), nicknamed the "Walkie-Talkie", widens as it rises to a three-floor sky garden. Its curved façade focused sunlight hot enough to melt cars on the street below, and in 2015 it won the Carbuncle Cup for the worst new building in the UK. In Uruguay the Laguna Garzón Bridge (2015) splits the road into a ring of separate lanes to cross a sensitive coastal lagoon.

name: Raili Pietilä
bio:
Raili Pietilä (1926–2021), born Raili Paatelainen, was a Finnish architect who did most of her work with her husband, Reima Pietilä; from 1963 all their buildings were credited to "Raili and Reima Pietilä". She graduated in architecture from the Helsinki University of Technology in 1956. In 1960 she and Reima Pietilä opened a joint office, renamed Raili and Reima Pietilä architects in 1975, and they married in 1963. A major exhibition of their work, "Challenging Modern Architecture", was held at the Museum of Finnish Architecture in 2008.

Their Kaleva Church in Tampere (1966) is built from 17 tall hollow concrete U-shapes, cast by slip-forming like a grain silo, with full-height windows between them and a plan shaped like a fish. The Metso Library in Tampere (1986), won in a 1978 competition, takes its name from the capercaillie it resembles from above, and its forms draw on Celtic patterns, animal shapes and glacial landforms. Mäntyniemi in Helsinki (1993) was the first official residence built for the President of Finland, set by the sea and finished inside in granite, birch and concrete.

name: Raymond Moriyama
bio:
Raymond Moriyama (1929–2023) was a Canadian architect whose Toronto practice, Moriyama & Teshima Architects, designed major buildings in Canada and abroad. Born in Vancouver, he was confined with his family to an internment camp in British Columbia's Slocan Valley during the Second World War, as Japanese Canadians were, and there built a tree house that he later called "my university, my place of solace". He studied at the University of Toronto and McGill, founded his firm in 1958, and was joined by Ted Teshima in 1970. He called his aim a humane architecture.

His first large independent work was the Ontario Science Centre in Toronto (1969), which opened as a hands-on science museum. The William G. Davis Building at the University of Toronto Mississauga (1973) and the Toronto Reference Library (1977), the largest public reference library in Canada, followed. The Bata Shoe Museum in Toronto (1995) is shaped like a shoe box, its tilted roof set askew like a lid. For the National Museum of Saudi Arabia in Riyadh (1999) he drew on the form and colour of the red sand dunes outside the city.

name: Reima Pietilä
bio:
Reima Pietilä (1923–1993) was a Finnish architect and theorist who did most of his work with his wife, Raili Pietilä; from 1963 all their buildings were credited to "Raili and Reima Pietilä". Born in Turku, where a school friend was the future president Mauno Koivisto, he graduated from the Helsinki University of Technology in 1953. His career took off when he won the competition for the Finnish Pavilion at the 1958 Brussels World's Fair. Widely read in philosophy and literature, he saw his work as organic and modern, wrote about the meaning of place, Finnish identity and even the Finnish language as a source of form.

Two competition wins followed in 1966: the Kaleva Church in Tampere and Dipoli, the student union building at Otaniemi in Espoo, built of pine, copper and natural rock with 500 windows of which only four are the same. The Metso Library in Tampere (1986) and Lieksa Church (1982) came later, along with work in Kuwait and New Delhi. Mäntyniemi in Helsinki (1993), the presidential residence, was finished in the year of his death, and Koivisto was its first resident.

name: Riken Yamamoto
bio:
Riken Yamamoto (born 1945) is a Japanese architect who received the Pritzker Prize in 2024. Born in Beijing to Japanese parents, he returned with his family to Japan in 1947 and grew up in Yokohama. He studied at Nihon University and the Tokyo University of the Arts and then under Hiroshi Hara at the University of Tokyo, and in 1973 founded his office, Riken Yamamoto & Field Shop. The Pritzker jury, chaired by Alejandro Aravena, praised the way he blurs "the boundary between public and private" to create conditions for community, calling him "a reassuring architect who brings dignity to everyday life".

His most representative works include housing in Yokohama and Tokyo, such as the Rotunda Building (1981) and the Hamlet (1988). Later came university work, among it a research building at Future University Hakodate (2000). The Yokosuka Museum of Art (2007), in a coastal park in Kanagawa, won the Japan Institute of Architects Award. His later works include The Circle at Zurich Airport (2020).

name: Schmidt Hammer Lassen
bio:
Schmidt Hammer Lassen is an international architecture firm founded in Aarhus, Denmark, in 1986 by Morten Schmidt, Bjarne Hammer and John F. Lassen. It has offices in Copenhagen, Aarhus and Shanghai, and in 2018 became part of the global firm Perkins and Will. Libraries are at the heart of its work, from Copenhagen and Aarhus to Ningbo and Shanghai, along with museums and the permanent premises of the International Criminal Court in The Hague (2015).

The firm's first major project was Katuaq, the culture centre in Nuuk, Greenland (1997), raised above the ground and clad inside and out in golden larch behind a screen inspired by the northern lights. It then won the international competition for the extension of the Royal Danish Library on Copenhagen's harbourfront, the Black Diamond (1999), named for its polished black granite and irregular angles. ARoS Aarhus Kunstmuseum (2004) later gained Olafur Eliasson's circular skywalk, Your rainbow panorama. Dokk1 in Aarhus (2015), which combines a library and other civic uses under one roof, was named Public Library of the Year in 2016, and the firm also designed Tūranga (Christchurch Central Library) (2018) in New Zealand.

name: Terunobu Fujimori
bio:
Terunobu Fujimori (born 1946) is a Japanese architect and architectural historian, known for odd, humorous buildings made with natural materials and old techniques used in new ways. Born in what is now Chino in Nagano Prefecture, he studied at Tōhoku University and the University of Tokyo, where he later became a professor. In the 1970s he led the "Architecture Detectives", who searched Tokyo for early Western-style buildings. He did not begin to build until his forties, with a historical museum in his home town in 1991, and he became widely known in the West after representing Japan at the 2006 Venice Biennale.

The Nira House (Leek House) in Machida (1997), planted with leeks, won the Japan Grand Art Prix, and the Akino Fuku Art Museum in Hamamatsu (1998) followed. Takasugi-an (2004), whose name means "too high tea house", sits six metres up on two chestnut trees and is entered by ladder. Lamune Onsen in Taketa (2005) is a hot-spring bath faced in bands of charred cedar and white mortar, its steam towers roofed in hand-rolled copper and each topped with a live pine.

name: Togo Murano
bio:
Togo Murano (1891–1984) was a Japanese architect, recognised as a master of the modern sukiya style, who completed more than three hundred projects in a career that lasted until his death. He studied electrical engineering and then architecture at Waseda University, graduating in 1918, and spent eleven years in Osaka in the office of Setsu Watanabe before starting his own practice in 1929. Rather than follow one style, he used the sukiya tradition, with its attention to surfaces, contrasting materials and fine detail, to join Japanese tradition with elements borrowed from the West.

The Memorial Cathedral for World Peace in Hiroshima (1954) replaced a cathedral destroyed by the atomic bomb; Murano, a juror in the competition, ended up designing it, with a concrete frame filled with rough bricks made from earth containing ash from the bomb. Yokohama City Hall (1959 building) followed. The Nissay Theatre (Nippon Life Hibiya Building) in Tokyo (1963) has a ceiling encrusted with mother-of-pearl, an example of the sukiya attention to surfaces in his work. His later projects introduced angular motifs, circular plans and curves, as at the Tanimura Art Museum in Itoigawa (1983).

name: Vilanova Artigas
bio:
João Batista Vilanova Artigas (1915–1985) was a Brazilian modernist architect, counted among the most important figures in the architecture of São Paulo and the founding figure of the Paulista School. Born in Curitiba, he graduated from the Polytechnic School of the University of São Paulo in 1937, and received a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1946. A member of the Brazilian Communist Party, he was removed from his teaching post in 1969, as was Paulo Mendes da Rocha, and both were reinstated in the 1980s.

His work is usually seen in three phases: early houses influenced by Frank Lloyd Wright, a move to the International Style with curtain walls and pilotis after 1945, and from the 1960s a dramatic personal style linked to brutalism for large public buildings. The Edifício Louveira (1949), a housing complex, and the Second Artigas House (Residência Vilanova Artigas II) (1949), his own home, belong to the second phase. The Morumbi Stadium (Estádio Cícero Pompeu de Toledo) (1970) is marked by the city as a monument of Brazilian modernism, and the FAU-USP Building (1969), for the university's architecture school, is one of the main works of Brazilian modernism.

name: Vladimir Shukhov
bio:
Vladimir Shukhov (1853–1939) was a Russian and Soviet engineer, scientist and architect whose new methods of structural analysis led to the world's first hyperboloid structures, diagrid shells, tensile structures and gridshells. Born in Graivoron, in today's Belgorod Oblast, he graduated with a gold medal from the Imperial Moscow Technical School in 1876, turned down a post teaching mathematics, and became chief engineer of a new engineering company. Besides oil tanks, pipelines and the first cracking process, he invented a family of doubly curved, lightweight forms based on hyperboloids of revolution, together with the mathematics to calculate them, and built about 200 hyperboloid towers. His honours included the Lenin Prize (1929).

The Adziogol Lighthouse near Kherson in Ukraine (1911) is a lattice hyperboloid of steel bars that still guides ships into the Dnieper estuary. The Shukhov Tower in Moscow (1922), a 160-metre steel diagrid radio mast, was built during the Russian Civil War, and the Shukhov Tower on the Oka River (1929) carried power lines near Nizhny Novgorod. With Konstantin Melnikov he engineered the Bakhmetevsky Bus Garage (1928) and the Novo-Ryazanskaya Street Bus Garage (1929) in Moscow, both Constructivist works.

name: Walter Gropius
bio:
Walter Gropius (1883–1969) was a German-American architect, founder of the Bauhaus and one of the pioneering masters of modernist architecture. Born in Berlin, he studied in Munich and Berlin and in 1908 joined the office of Peter Behrens before setting up his own practice with Adolf Meyer in 1910. In 1919 he became head of the school in Weimar that he turned into the Bauhaus, leading it until 1928. He left Germany for England in 1934 and the United States in 1937, where he taught at the Harvard Graduate School of Design and won the AIA Gold Medal in 1959.

The Fagus Factory in Alfeld (1911), whose façade he designed with Meyer, was one of the first modernist buildings, with glass curtain walls. When the Bauhaus moved to Dessau he designed its new home, Bauhaus Dessau (1926), whose workshop wing is wrapped in glass. In America his own Gropius House in Lincoln, Massachusetts (1938) helped bring modernism to the country, and the MetLife Building in New York (1963), designed with Pietro Belluschi as the Pan Am Building, was among his last large works.

name: Welton Becket
bio:
Welton Becket (1902–1969) was an American modernist architect who designed many buildings in Los Angeles and built one of the largest architecture offices in the world. Born in Seattle, he studied at the University of Washington and in 1933 moved to Los Angeles, where his partnership's first major commission was the Pan-Pacific Auditorium (1935). With his partner Walter Wurdeman he developed the idea of "total design", in which the firm handled everything from master plan and engineering to interiors, furniture and signs. After Wurdeman's death in 1949 he led Welton Becket and Associates.

Parker Center in Los Angeles (1955), the police headquarters, has since been demolished. The Capitol Records Building in Hollywood (1956), designed by Louis Naidorf in Becket's office, is considered the world's first circular office building and looks like a stack of records on a turntable. In 1958 came the Santa Monica Civic Auditorium and the 27-storey Hotel Habana Libre (former Habana Hilton) in Havana, which Fidel Castro used as his residence in 1959. His firm continued after his death and designed Reunion Tower in Dallas (1978), topped by a geodesic sphere.

name: WOHA
bio:
WOHA is a Singapore architecture and industrial design firm founded in 1994 by Wong Mun Summ and Richard Hassell, its name taken from the first two letters of each surname. The two met at Kerry Hill Architects and began with private houses, then turned to public and commercial work after winning two competitions for Singapore metro stations in 2000. Its high-rise buildings use planting as a building material and stay open to the breeze to reduce air conditioning, an approach the firm calls "breathing architecture", aimed at better living in dense tropical cities. The 1 Moulmein Rise condominium won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 2007.

The Met in Bangkok (2009), a residential tower, won the International Highrise Award and the RIBA Lubetkin Award, whose jury saw it as proof "that an alternative strategy to the sleek air-conditioned box can work in the tropics". The Parkroyal Collection Pickering hotel (2013) carries 15,000 square metres of terraced "sky gardens", and the Oasia Hotel Downtown (2016) wraps its tower in aluminium mesh supporting more than 50 species of plants.

name: Achyut Kanvinde
bio:
Achyut Kanvinde (1916–2002) was an Indian architect whose functional buildings carry elements of brutalism. Born in Achra in the Konkan region of Maharashtra, he graduated in architecture from the Sir J. J. School of Art in Bombay in 1942. The Government of India then sent him to Harvard, where he studied under Walter Gropius; he later said he owed Gropius "a tremendous debt" for opening his eyes to technology and to the psychology of space. Back in India he worked for the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research and founded the firm Kanvinde, Rai and Chowdhury in New Delhi with Shaukat Rai. He received the Padma Shri in 1974.

He paid close attention to natural light, ventilation and heat, and supported vernacular building. The ATIRA (Ahmedabad Textile Industry's Research Association) complex (1954) was an early commission. His firm designed the IIT Kanpur Academic Area (c. 1966) and many dairy buildings, including the Dudhsagar Dairy in Mehsana (1970), a brutalist plant for a farmers' cooperative. The ISKCON Temple (Glory of India) in New Delhi (1998) is a late example of his play with space and form.

name: Alberto Campo Baeza
bio:
Alberto Campo Baeza (born 1946) is a Spanish architect and teacher, often grouped with David Chipperfield and John Pawson among architects associated with minimalism. Born in Valladolid, he graduated from the Polytechnic University of Madrid in 1971, took his doctorate in 1982, and was professor of design at the Madrid school of architecture from 1986 to 2017. He favours white and neutral colour to bring out natural light, and in 2024 he received the Daylight Award.

Much of his work is houses: Casa Gaspar in Vejer de la Frontera (1992), set in Cádiz province, and Casa De Blas at Sevilla la Nueva near Madrid (2000), which won the COAM Award in 2002. In Granada the Caja Granada Headquarters (2001) won the Eduardo Torroja Award, and the Museum of Memory of Andalusia (MA) (2009) was nominated for the Mies van der Rohe Award and honoured at the Buenos Aires Biennial. Later works include the House of the Infinite in Cádiz (2014). Alberto Campo Baeza's buildings are studied for light, proportion and economy of means.

name: Architectus
bio:
Architectus is an architecture and design practice with 13 studios across Australia and New Zealand, from Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane to Auckland and Christchurch. With more than 800 architects, interior designers, landscape architects, urban planners and other specialists, it describes itself as the largest practice in its region. Its work covers commercial, defence, infrastructure, public and transport projects, with education and health as its two largest areas, and many of its buildings were designed together with partners from abroad.

Early landmarks include the Gallery of Modern Art in Brisbane (2006). 1 Bligh Street in Sydney (2011), an office tower designed with the German firm Ingenhoven Architects, has a naturally ventilated atrium running its full 120-metre height and won the International High Rise Award in 2012. The Queen Elizabeth II Courts of Law in Brisbane (2012) won the Australian Institute of Architects' national award for public architecture in 2013. With SANAA the practice worked on the Art Gallery of New South Wales, North Building (Sydney Modern, Naala Nura) (2022), which won a national award for public architecture in 2023.

name: Artur Tarkhanyan
bio:
Artur Tarkhanyan (1932–2006) was a Soviet Armenian architect who designed public buildings and memorials in Yerevan, usually as one of a small team of Armenian architects. He was named an Honoured Architect of the Armenian SSR in 1972 and received the Armenian SSR State Prize in 1985 and the USSR State Prize in 1987.

The Armenian Genocide Memorial at Tsitsernakaberd (1967), designed with Sashur Kalashyan and the artist Hovhannes Khachatryan, sets 12 inward-leaning stone slabs in a circle around an eternal flame, beside a 44-metre memorial column split in two to express the rebirth of the nation. After a competition in 1970 he was one of the six architects chosen to design the Zvartnots Airport Old Terminal (1980). The Karen Demirchyan Sports and Concert Complex (1983), shaped like a great bird opening its wings, has a turning stand of 1,008 seats that joins the arena and concert hall, an idea that won its architects the USSR State Prize.

name: Ashton Raggatt McDougall
bio:
Ashton Raggatt McDougall, known as ARM Architecture, is an Australian architecture firm founded in Melbourne in 1988 by Stephen Ashton, Howard Raggatt and Ian McDougall, with further offices in Sydney and Adelaide. Its work has been described as "architectural outspokenness": buildings that borrow patterns from mathematics and puzzles. Besides new buildings it has taken on heritage and renewal work, such as the refurbishment of Hamer Hall and the redevelopment of the Shrine of Remembrance in Melbourne, and master plans for Melbourne Docklands and Elizabeth Quay in Perth. By 2016 it was the only Australian firm to have won the Australian Institute of Architects' Premier State Award seven times.

RMIT Storey Hall in Melbourne (1995) adds an annex to a historic hall, its street front and its auditorium covered in Penrose tiling in green and purple. The National Museum of Australia in Canberra (2001) and the Melbourne Recital Centre (2009), built with the Southbank Theatre, are among its best-known public buildings. Perth Arena (2012), whose angular form is based on the Eternity puzzle, holds up to 15,000 people for concerts.

name: Behnisch & Partner
bio:
Behnisch & Partner was the Stuttgart architecture practice of Günter Behnisch (1922–2010), who opened his office in 1952 and renamed it Behnisch & Partner in 1966. Born near Dresden, Behnisch served in the German navy in the Second World War, becoming one of its youngest U-boat commanders, and after the war trained as a bricklayer before studying architecture in Stuttgart from 1947. He became one of the best-known German architects associated with deconstructivism. His son Stefan Behnisch set up a separate firm, Behnisch Architekten, in 1989.

In 1967 the practice was chosen to plan the park for the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich. For the Munich Olympic Stadium (1972), Behnisch worked with the engineer Frei Otto on a light tent roof of acrylic glass held by steel cables, one of the first of its kind at this scale and a symbol of the "cheerful Games". The Plenary Building of the Bundestag, Bonn (1992), won in a 1973 competition but begun only in 1987, became the new home of West Germany's parliament. The Norddeutsche Landesbank (NORD/LB) Headquarters in Hanover (2002) came at the end of Behnisch's career.
